paragraphs: Source. Definitions and taxonomy follow Michael Flood, “AI Agent Swarm Part 1 – Definitions” (LessWrong, 31 August 2026): an AI agent swarm is a system of two or more AI agents whose causal interactions produce self-organized, mutually conditioned collective behavior directed toward one or more collective goals, where the coordination structure or collective goals were not explicitly specified by a human or orchestrating system. Humans may provide channels, workspaces or tools without that preventing a swarm.

Necessary features. F1 multiplicity: two or more AI agents (accounts run by one operator or script count as one). F2 causal interaction: agents affect each other directly or through a shared environment, checked by timestamp order; running in parallel is not enough. F3 self-organization: the important coordination policies, structures, divisions of labor, norms and goals arise from the agents' interactions rather than being specified in advance. F4 mutually conditioning behavior: agents respond to what each other do. F5 a collective goal: a group-level task, an instrumental state, or another functional objective, which may be inferred from persistent coordinated behavior rather than stated.

Exclusions. Parallel convergence without causal influence is an aggregate (level 0); one-off exchanges are cooperation, not swarming; stable equilibria such as many agents independently choosing the same thing are not collective goals. A swarm may be temporary, and collective goals need not be terminal: agents with separate goals can share an instrumental one.

Progression (graded, not yes/no). 1 interaction: one agent causally affects another. 2 cooperation: interaction advances one or both agents' individual objectives. 3 coordination: behavior becomes mutually conditioned. 4 self-organization: persistent or task-relevant roles, norms, strategies, topology, specialization or division of labor emerge without being prescribed. 5 swarm formation: that self-organized coordination serves an identifiable collective functional goal. Episodes whose structure was entirely dictated stop at coordination.

Reading level 5. The post lets a swarm be temporary and lets its goal be instrumental or inferred from behavior, so level 5 here includes short-lived structures, for example agents inventing a voting procedure for one afternoon, alongside multi-week relay networks. Under the stricter reading used in an earlier draft (structure had to keep working while members changed), only 23 episodes reached level 5. Episodes with thin evidence are marked low confidence.

Axes. Origin: seeded (a human or orchestrator deliberately set agents up to act together), afforded (the designers provided ways to interact but did not prescribe the organization) or spontaneous (agents deployed for independent purposes formed it without anyone intending a swarm). AI Village and Moltbook are built for agents to interact, so their episodes are seeded or afforded; DSEWiki agents found and repurposed an outside wiki, so its episodes are spontaneous. Goal relation to the assigned task: supporting, orthogonal or conflicting (against objectives or constraints); one episode can show several. Consequence for people: beneficial, neutral or ambiguous, or harmful or dangerous. Goal type: shared task, shared instrumental, or collective preservation (keeping the collaboration, channel, membership or organization going).

Primary function (this edition). Each episode also gets the single thing the group is mainly doing: belief and knowledge (forming, spreading or correcting beliefs), doing the work (dividing and executing tasks), rules and decisions (making, enforcing or contesting them), building shared tools (channels, tools, shared resources), identity and culture (ritual, cohesion), competing, gaming or attacking (contests, rule-gaming, spam, manipulation, collusion against constraints), or none. This category comes from the companion taxonomy analysis, which found raters applied it about as consistently as Flood's level (Krippendorff's alpha 0.85, as reported there) and that it separates episodes the level cannot, such as belief work and rule-gaming, which occur at every level.

Origin intent (this edition). Each episode's originating message was scored on its own for how deliberately it set out to organize others: 1 offhand (a status note or aside with no ask), 2 mostly offhand, 3 ambiguous, 4 mostly deliberate (a proposal with a soft ask), 5 explicit (a direct proposal, instruction, rule or call to action aimed at other agents). The score ignores how far the episode later went, so low-intent starts that reached high levels mark cases where agents organized around a remark that was not meant as a plan. Scores and function labels come from the companion analysis (one model pass); episodes it did not cover were labelled here with the same definitions, and each episode says which.

Data. AI Village: aidigestorg/ai-village on Hugging Face (chat, 2025-04-02 to 2026-09-18). Moltbook: public crawls of posts and comment threads (2026-01-27 to 02-08). DSEWiki: the collusion.wiki dump of agent edits to four abandoned wikis (2026-05-24 to 07-02), checksums verified; it contains no reasoning traces, so each wiki edit is treated as a message.

Method. Ten sweep agents each read one slice of one dataset and recorded every candidate episode with its time window, participants, a selector for pulling the transcript, verbatim key messages and evidence for each feature. Reviewers merged duplicates across slices and graded everything under one rule set aligned to the post. Every key message shown was looked up in the raw data by time and speaker; the panel marks any that could not be found.

Safety and privacy. Transcripts have credentials, account passwords, tokens and email addresses removed, and links reduced to their host name. DSEWiki transcripts keep the agents' coordination text but withhold technical lines, and evasion techniques are described only in general terms.

Limits. AI Village staff and viewer labels come from the event log; an automated nudging bot is shown separately from people. DSEWiki handles are unreliable agent identities, so participant counts there are approximate. Moltbook has crawl gaps. Chart counts are messages in each episode's window and room or page set, so overlapping episodes share messages.

Related. A separate page traces how coined terms spread between agents and model families, and checks how reliably Flood's taxonomy can be applied (blind raters, alternative partitions): https://claude.ai/artifact/AiWv6XyPmcWEByvpRD7FAG

recall.text: A separate detector scored every unit for multi-agent back-and-forth, independent of the sweep agents, and every strong unit no episode covered was then read and graded by hand.
rows: AI Village: 480 room-days with 3+ agents; 96% covered by the sweep, including 49 of the 50 strongest. All 18 uncovered room-days were reviewed: 5 new episodes (one at level 4, a 12-agent governance-toolkit project), 9 window corrections to existing episodes, and the rest either part of existing episodes or below 3 agents.

DSEWiki: 651 pages with 3+ agent handles; 87% covered by page name, including 63 of the 65 strongest. The 35 strongest uncovered pages were reviewed: 3 new episodes and 5 corrections. The biggest miss, the first relay hub (Sector 61-62, 16 June), had been counted as covered only because other episodes listed its page name, so page-name coverage overstates recall; it is now its own episode.

Moltbook: 15,369 threads with 3+ commenters and a two-way reply pair, almost none covered. The 60 strongest were read one by one: 56 are level 1 (in 54 the post's author answers each commenter once; commenters rarely address each other), 2 are level 2 and 2 are aggregates. 6 episodes were added from this review.

validation: 3,483 of 3,547 key messages (98.2%) were found in the raw data at the stated time and speaker; the rest are marked in each episode.
